What do you know of their effort and where do you stand on their effort?

And if Speaker Boehner had brought that up, although there was opposition within his conference, I believe there were 60-80 Republicans that were voted for it, and there were certainly 180 Democrats, and most of these immigration issues that we're dealing with today with this broken system would have been resolved, not that it was a perfect bill. Now we're going back to trying to deal with immigration reform in various pieces The effort that my colleagues Olafgren and Jimmy Benetta are engaged in I think are very important. Hearing will take place next week among agricultural representatives and farm labor representatives. What we have to do as members of the Agriculture Committee, and as the Chairman of the Subcommittee on Livestock and Foreign Trade, is to ensure that not only those farming today, but the next generation of farmers, and one of the things that concerns me is the ability to pass on that family farm and to keep the next generation motivated and focusing on agriculture, because the age of the average American farmers getting up there and that's worrisome for Maine. turn_text: Certainly you mentioned the implementation of the new Farm Bill and obviously dairy policy is one that was much needed. Do you think this policy that's been approved is adequate or are we just in a reality phase of economics of scale making it difficult for the small dairy producer?

Well, that's a question that's going to be asked on our subcommittee hearing at the end of April after the Easter break that will be on the impacts of the losses that dairy producers around the country have faced. And it's just not small producers. It's the midsize and larger producers as well. We've had over 200 dairies go out of business in California in the last five years. This is where some of the largest areas are in the country. The equity that has been lost in the American area industry is I've been told by some approaching $20 billion and more. So the farm bill that we created obviously we think is very helpful to small dairies. And we are trying to provide additional support for all dairy producers. regardless of their size. But it is a very difficult set of circumstances when input costs in the dairy business vary anywhere from $12 to $14 per hundred weight in some places, $16 to $18 per hundred weight. and you know you can only stay in business so long when your input costs exceed the amount that you receive on a monthly basis. It's a challenge and so the hearing that we're going to be holding in late April, we're going to be looking to see the impacts that small dairies and dairies of all sizes are filling around the country and how much help this new farm bill will be and its implementation to dealing with some of those challenges of these these input costs and whether or not they can successfully stay in business.

turn_text: Speaking of hearings, one of the most contentious issues out of the development of the 18 bill was work requirements for those that would receive SNAP benefits. It seems the administration is moving ahead with that through the Department of Agriculture and Representative Fudge is having a hearing on that in a week ahead. What are your thoughts on this issue?

Well, everybody should be encouraged in this country to work. And I think that's a part of any constructive person that wants to succeed, right? But we know whether it's through seasonal employment or whether it's the working poor, or folks that have a 40-hour work week that are reduced to 20 hours a week, that food stamps, i.e. the SNAP program, is America's safety net. And the work requirements that were offered by my Republican colleagues in the House Ag Committee were simply not workable, period. And so Congresswoman Wedge has a real sense of this. We established five years ago when this issue was very open and focused. pilot projects that started here in California, and we've expanded to nine other states in which we've looked at the underlying causes of trying to get healthy, able-bodied people between the ages of 18 and 55 off of assistance and becoming self-sufficient. And what have we found? Well, the majority of those between that age group, 18 and 55, able-bodied, don't have a high school diploma. the majority of them have children. And so to ensure that they get on their feet, you've got to have an effort to ensure that they get the education necessary so that they can get a good-paying job that makes them self-sufficient. And when they're getting their education, as you're looking to get them into job placement, There's got to be an issue of childcare because if they don't have the ability to take care of their children, they certainly can't get the education necessary and the job training to get them on their feet. That's just the reality. And these 10 pilot projects in 10 various states across the country are verifying that. And seeing under the theory of one size doesn't fit all, how's the best way to deal with trying to make sure that we maintain a safety net for working poor people, and at the same time, create the opportunities for them to become self-sufficient and no longer in need of assistance.
